headline: Daibubun is 大 (dai, “big, great”) plus 部分 (bubun, “part, portion”), first attested in 1903.
Bunbōgu is 文房 (bunbō, “a study, an office”) plus 具 (-gu, “instrument, tool; means; ingredient”).
Waki began as a noun from 分く (waku, “to split, to divide”): the space where two things split apart, then “side”.
Kagu, “to smell”, is likely a verbalization of 香 (ka, “scent”), like 担ぐ (katagu) and 騒ぐ (sawagu).
Penki is borrowed from Dutch pek, ultimately from Latin pīx.
Urayamu, “to envy”, is 心 (ura, “heart, inner feelings”) plus 病む (yamu, “affected, afflicted, worried”).
Hikaku is 比 (hi, “to compare”) plus 較 (kaku, “to compare”): “compare” twice.
Takara, “treasure”, was analyzed as 高 (taka-, “high”) plus a pluralizing suffix, but the page calls that semantically problematic.
Tora is “anomalous”: Old Japanese to₁ra where the expected form was *tura.
Kushin is 苦 (ku, “hard, energetically”) plus 心 (shin, “heart”).
Kei, “plan”, is from Middle Chinese 計.
Sakuin, an index, is 索 (saku, “search for”) plus 引 (in, “quote, cite”).
Oi is the continuative stem of 老いる (oiru, “to age, to grow old”).
Ge, “lowness”, is from Middle Chinese 下.
Nigiru, which also covers moulding sushi, is from Old Japanese, derived from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *ninkiru.
Saichū, “in the middle of”, is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 中 (chū, “middle”).
De is the continuative stem of 出る (deru, “to come out”).
Chūō is a Middle Chinese compound, glossed literally as “centre”.
Mannaka is 真ん (man-, “true, real, exactly”) plus 中 (naka, “center, middle”).
Chansu is from English chance, first attested in 1893.
Tetsuzuki is 手 (te) plus 続き (tsuzuki).
Katamuku began as katabuku: the b lost its plosive and became a nasal m.
Hikakuteki is 比較 (hikaku, “comparison”) plus 的 (-teki, “-y”).
Taiko is a Sino-Japanese compound of 太 (tai, “big, fat, thick”) and 鼓 (ko, “drum”).
Wakareru is from Old Japanese wakaru, and cognate with 分かれる (wakareru) and 分ける (wakeru).
Tearai, a restroom, is 手 (te, “hand”) plus 洗い (arai, “washing”).
Kaku, “nucleus”, is from Middle Chinese 核.
Tataku is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tatak-, and cognate with Okinawan tatachun.
En, “chance, tie”, is from Middle Chinese 緣.
Obentō is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 弁当 (bentō, “bento”).
Namaiki is 生 (nama-, “raw → inexperienced, saucy”) plus 意気 (iki, “spirit”).
